gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the seasons, from winter snow and road closures to lush summer coasts and vibrant fall foliage.
gemini.overview: Acadia National Park is known for its rugged Atlantic coastline, where granite cliffs meet the ocean. Visitors drive or hike to the summit of Cadillac Mountain for sweeping views of the islands and sea, or walk the carriage roads around Jordan Pond. The scenery peaks in October when the forests turn bright red and gold.

blurbs.text: Most of the Park Loop Road is closed to cars, but the snow-covered granite shores and frozen lakes offer quiet, stark coastal views for those on foot or skis.
Melting snow and spring rain fill the streams, and the forests are still mostly bare. The Park Loop Road typically reopens by mid-April, restoring access to the major viewpoints.
Spring melt keeps the streams full and the forests turn green. The Park Loop Road and the drive up Cadillac Mountain are open for the coastal and island views.
The coastal views are clear and the forests are lush. The drive up Cadillac Mountain and the trails around Jordan Pond show off the rocky shores and deep blue water.
Early fall color brightens the hardwood forests, and the air is clear over the granite cliffs and the ocean.
The hardwood forests are at peak color in orange, red and yellow, a vivid contrast to the dark granite cliffs and the ocean.
The autumn leaves have fallen, leaving the forests bare. The scenery is muted, and late in the month, sections of the main park roads close for the winter season.

gemini.depth_why: The cliffs stay the same, but winter storms and swells limit the boat trips and the clarity.
gemini.overview: The Algarve is known for its Atlantic coastline of steep limestone cliffs, enclosed coves, and golden rock formations. The sea stacks and arches of Ponta da Piedade rise directly from the water, creating a maze of stone pillars. Nearby, the Benagil cave features a natural oculus that frames the sky above an interior beach.

blurbs.text: Winter storms bring gray skies and heavy swells, so boat trips to the sea caves run only on calm days. The cliffs and sea stacks are still clear from the headland trails.
Wildflowers cover the clifftops, showers pass quickly, and boats to the sea caves run on most days.
Clear skies and calm seas show the golden cliffs and sea stacks at their sharpest, and boat and kayak trips reach the caves most days.
The light is warm and the seas are mostly calm, though the first autumn storms can cancel boat trips to the caves.

gemini.depth_why: Scores peak in spring for the bulb fields, while the rest of the year is grouped by daylight hours for viewing the canals.
gemini.overview: Amsterdam's landscapes are defined by the vast network of historic canals shaping the city center. Beyond the urban waterways, the surrounding flatlands transform in spring when massive fields of tulips and other bulbs bloom in bright, geometric stripes.

blurbs.text: Short winter days mean the sun sets early, but the canal rings remain the focal point of the landscape. The waterways reflect the lights of the bridges in the early evenings, and occasional winter frosts can leave a thin layer of ice on the smaller canals.
Daffodils and hyacinths color the bulb fields just outside the city, and the canal rings are lined with budding trees. Lengthening days give more time for evening walks along the water.

Millions of tulips, daffodils and hyacinths bloom in the fields just outside the city, creating vast stripes of bright color across the flat landscape. The canal rings are lined with fresh green trees.
Long evenings leave plenty of daylight to take in the canal rings. The water reflects the historic bridges and tall, narrow houses, and the trees lining the waterways are in full leaf.
The trees lining the canals are at autumn gold, reflected in the water beside the historic bridges and tall, narrow houses.
The trees along the canals are mostly bare, and the short days bring early lamplight to the water and the historic bridges.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise in spring and early summer when the landscape is greenest, dip slightly in the heat of late summer, and fall in winter.
gemini.overview: The region's signature views blend dramatic natural settings with historic architecture, most famously the Alhambra against the Sierra Nevada and the Pueblos Blancos of Cadiz and Malaga provinces, including Ronda, split in two by its famous El Tajo gorge. Spring and early summer offer the clearest skies and greenest hillsides before the intense heat of late summer dries the terrain.

blurbs.text: Winter brings cooler temperatures and occasional rain, turning the hillsides green. The Sierra Nevada mountains are often capped with snow, providing a striking backdrop to the Alhambra, though some higher mountain passes may be closed.
The hills and valleys are green after the winter rains, and the Sierra Nevada still shows snow above the whitewashed villages. Temperatures are comfortable for driving the routes between them.

Green hills and clear weather suit driving between the whitewashed villages. The coastal cliffs and the deep El Tajo gorge in Ronda are easy to reach, with warm temperatures for walking the viewpoints.

The landscape dries out under intense sun, turning the rolling hills golden and brown. The arid badlands of the Tabernas Desert look their most stark, while the coastal views remain clear, though the heat makes long walks less comfortable.
The landscape is still dry, with golden-brown hills and the stark badlands of the Tabernas Desert. The coastal views remain clear, and temperatures are easier for walking the viewpoints.

gemini.depth_why: Scores fall into three distinct seasons based on the monsoon cycle and visibility.
gemini.overview: Cambodia is known for the jungle reclaiming ancient stone and the vast floodplains of the Mekong River. The signature views are the massive strangler figs overtaking the ruins of Ta Prohm and the silhouette of Angkor Wat at sunrise. Beyond the temple complexes, the landscape features flat rice paddies, the dense forests of the Cardamom Mountains, and the seasonal filling of Tonle Sap lake.

blurbs.text: Clear skies provide the best conditions for the famous temple sunrise. The countryside is still relatively green from the recent rains, and dry dirt roads make it easy to reach remote jungle temples and the Cardamom Mountains.

The rice paddies and rural landscapes are brown and dusty. Agricultural burning often creates a haze that washes out the sky and obscures distant views, though the jungle around Ta Prohm stays shaded.

Monsoon rains turn the country a vibrant, lush green and swell the waters of Tonle Sap lake. Heavy cloud cover frequently blocks sunrises, and frequent downpours turn unpaved rural routes into thick mud, limiting access to remote areas.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with access and visibility due to winter snow and summer heat.
gemini.overview: The draw here is the desert and canyon scenery, known for more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches, deep gorges, and towering mesas. Delicate Arch at sunset and Mesa Arch at dawn are the signature views, while the Island in the Sky district offers sweeping overlooks of the canyon country. The landscape is best seen in spring and fall, when temperatures allow for longer hikes and drives.

blurbs.text: Winter brings cold temperatures and occasional snow, which can temporarily close roads and trails. The contrast of white snow against red rock is striking, but access to some viewpoints may be limited.
Spring warms the desert and the snow melts from the trails and scenic drives, leaving the views clear.
The weather is ideal for exploring the viewpoints and hiking to the arches. The clear skies and mild temperatures make this the prime time to see the canyons and rock formations.
Summer heat can be intense, making midday hikes to the arches difficult. The scenery stays in clear view, but early morning or late evening visits are the comfortable way to reach the viewpoints.
Temperatures cool down, giving ideal conditions for hiking and driving through the parks. The clear autumn air provides excellent visibility across the vast canyon landscapes.
Colder weather and the possibility of snow mark late fall and early winter. The main roads usually stay clear, but some trails to the arches may be icy or harder to reach.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with distinct summer access, autumn colors, winter snow, and spring snowmelt.
gemini.overview: The Argentine Lake District is known for deep glacial lakes set against the forested peaks of the Andes. The Seven Lakes Road and Circuito Chico drives connect these water bodies, providing continuous views of mountains, rivers and dense forests.

blurbs.text: Clear roads and dry trails allow full access to high mountain passes and remote lake shores. The long daylight hours provide ample time for driving the major scenic routes.
The lenga and ñire forests turn bright red and yellow, contrasting sharply with the blue lakes. Rain increases late in the season, and low clouds can occasionally obscure the higher peaks.
Snow covers the Andes and lower forests, completely altering the landscape. Shorter days and heavy snowfall restrict access to unpaved scenic routes and higher mountain viewpoints.
Heavy snowmelt swells the region's rivers and waterfalls to their highest volumes. The lower valleys turn green again, though high mountain passes often hold snow until late in the season.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery in Aruba is accessible and largely unchanged throughout the year.
gemini.overview: Aruba is known for its coasts, contrasting calm white-sand beaches with a rugged, arid eastern shore. Eagle Beach provides the classic Caribbean view of wide sand and clear water, while Arikok National Park covers much of the island with a dry landscape of cacti and limestone cliffs. The eastern coastline features natural bridges and crashing waves against the rock.

blurbs.text: The coastal views remain clear and accessible. The contrast between the calm western beaches and the rough, cactus-studded eastern shore in Arikok National Park is visible on drives and walks.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with snow cover, access to high passes, and autumn color.
gemini.overview: The Elk Mountains define the scenery here, anchored by the Maroon Bells, two 14,000-foot peaks reflected in a high alpine lake. The surrounding valleys hold dense forests of aspen trees that turn bright gold in autumn. High-elevation drives like Independence Pass offer sweeping views of the peaks and tundra, while winter brings deep snow cover to the slopes.

blurbs.text: Deep snow covers the peaks and valleys, turning the landscape into a winter scene. Independence Pass and the road to the Maroon Bells are closed to cars, but the snow-covered mountains are visible from the ski areas and town.
Snow begins to melt at lower elevations, leaving the landscape in transition. High passes and the road to the Maroon Bells remain closed to vehicles.
Spring green reaches the valleys, though snow remains on the high peaks. Independence Pass and the road to the Maroon Bells typically open late in the month, restoring access to the signature views.
The high country is wide open to visitors. The Maroon Bells are clear of snow and reflected in the lake, and Independence Pass gives drives above the tree line. The forests are deep green.
The aspen forests turn bright gold, contrasting with the evergreen pines and the gray rock of the peaks. Independence Pass and the Maroon Bells provide the most vivid views of the year.

The autumn leaves drop early in the month, and the first snows begin to dust the high peaks. The landscape transitions toward winter, and high-elevation roads may close temporarily or for the season depending on storms.

Snow begins to accumulate in the valleys, and the high passes, including Independence Pass and the road to the Maroon Bells, close for the winter. The scenery is stark before the deep winter snowpack builds.

gemini.depth_why: The Altiplanic winter slightly reduces access to high-altitude sites in January and February, separating them from the rest of the year.
gemini.overview: The Atacama Desert holds some of the most extreme arid landscapes on Earth. Visitors come for the jagged, salt-crusted rock formations of Moon Valley and the vast salt flats stretching toward volcanic horizons. High in the Andes, the bright blue Altiplanic lagoons sit beneath snow-capped peaks, while the El Tatio geysers send up thick columns of steam at dawn.

blurbs.text: Occasional rain and snow can reach the high Andes, and the moisture can temporarily close dirt roads to the high-altitude lagoons and geysers, though the lower valleys usually stay clear.
Dry, clear conditions keep the high-altitude dirt roads passable and the volcanic horizons sharp. The dry air gives dependable views of the geysers at dawn and the salt flats at sunset.

gemini.depth_why: The Acropolis stays the same, but summer heat and haze and winter rain affect the views.
gemini.overview: The defining landscape of the Greek capital is the Acropolis rising sharply above the dense urban sprawl. Viewpoints like Mount Lycabettus and Philopappos Hill offer sweeping panoramas of the ancient citadel set against the modern city and the distant Aegean Sea. The surrounding Attica region also provides modest coastal scenery along the Saronic Gulf.

blurbs.text: Rain and gray skies come and go, but clear days between them give crisp, sharp views of the Acropolis from Mount Lycabettus and Philopappos Hill.
Mild, clear days and green hillsides with wildflowers frame the Acropolis, and the trails up Mount Lycabettus and Philopappos Hill look across the white city to the sea.
Strong heat and haze soften the distant views, so the climbs up Mount Lycabettus and Philopappos Hill are best at sunrise and sunset, when the Acropolis glows above the city.
Warm, clear days and soft evening light show the Acropolis and the white sprawl of the capital stretching toward the Aegean.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise gradually from winter to summer as visibility improves and hydrangeas bloom.
gemini.overview: The Azores are known for volcanic calderas, crater lakes and dramatic green coastlines. The signature views are the twin lakes of Sete Cidades and the caldera of Lagoa do Fogo on São Miguel. Summer brings the best visibility and the famous blue hydrangeas that line the roads, particularly on Faial.

blurbs.text: Winter brings frequent rain, low clouds and fog that can obscure the higher viewpoints, including the crater lakes. The coastal scenery remains visible, though the seas are often rough.
Visibility is improving and the days are long enough for driving the coastal routes. The landscape is a bright green.
The first hydrangeas bloom along the roadsides, and long days give more time for the coastal routes and the crater lake viewpoints.
Summer offers the clearest skies for viewing the calderas and lakes from high vantage points. Blue hydrangeas are in full bloom along the roadsides and coastal cliffs.
Clear spells are still common and hydrangeas linger along some roadsides, though clouds can hide the mountain viewpoints.
Low clouds and frequent rain can hide the mountain viewpoints, and the waterfalls run full.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change as snow closes high-elevation scenic drives in winter and clears for full access in summer.
gemini.overview: The region contrasts the sharply eroded, banded buttes of the Badlands with the dark, pine-covered granite peaks of the Black Hills. Scenic drives such as the Needles Highway and Badlands Loop Road navigate narrow rock tunnels, steep canyons, and vast prairie overlooks.

blurbs.text: Snow often shuts high-elevation routes in the Black Hills, including the Needles Highway and Iron Mountain Road. The Badlands Loop Road usually remains plowed, showing the eroded desert pinnacles dusted in white.
The lower canyon roads are clear, and the high granite passes in the Black Hills are mostly open to drivers, though a late storm can shut them for a day.
All scenic routes are clear, allowing drives through the narrow rock tunnels of the Needles Highway and full access to the vast desert overlooks of the Badlands.
Yellow foliage colors the canyons of the Black Hills, and early snow can limit access to the highest mountain passes.
The foliage is gone, leaving dark pine against the granite of the Black Hills. Snow can limit access to the highest passes, though the Badlands Loop Road usually stays open.

gemini.depth_why: Scores follow the dry and wet seasons, with visibility and access dropping during the monsoon.
gemini.overview: The signature view of Myanmar is the plain of Bagan, where thousands of ancient temples rise from the dust, often seen at sunrise from a hot air balloon. Beyond the temples, Myanmar is known for the Irrawaddy River, the floating villages and leg-rowers of Inle Lake, and the limestone karst formations of Hpa-An. The scenery is best viewed during the dry, cooler months when skies are clear.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and dry weather make this the prime time to see the temples at sunrise, with hot air balloons flying at dawn. The waters of Inle Lake are calm, and the views of the surrounding hills and floating gardens are sharp.

Skies are mostly clear and the days are hot, with hot air balloons still flying over the temples at dawn. The views of the temples and the Irrawaddy River are sharp, though heat haze can soften the horizon by afternoon.
Heat builds across the plains, creating hazy conditions that can soften the views of the temples and the Irrawaddy River. Hot air balloon flights typically end their season as temperatures rise.
Hot days and the first heavy rains bring thick cloud that can hide the hills and temples, and dirt roads in rural areas turn muddy.
The monsoon brings heavy rain and thick cloud that obscure the hills and temples. Dirt roads in rural areas become muddy, making access to some viewpoints difficult.
Heavy monsoon rain washes out rural roads and keeps skies overcast. Visibility is low, and the Irrawaddy River swells, changing the landscape but making travel to viewpoints challenging.
Rain showers are still frequent, though the countryside is lush and green. Cloud often hides the hills and temples.
The rains ease and the countryside is lush and green, with skies clearing more often. Hot air balloon flights usually resume at the start of the month.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the wet and hurricane seasons as clouds and storms reduce water clarity.
gemini.overview: The Bahamas is known for its coastal scenery, where shallow sandbanks create distinctive turquoise and sapphire waters. The Exuma chain offers hundreds of small cays and sandbars, including the well-known beach at Big Major Cay. The clearest views and most vivid water colors align with the dry season.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and calm conditions maximize water clarity, making the shallow banks and cays highly visible. The vivid blues of the ocean contrast sharply with the white sandbars.
Humidity rises and brief showers become more common, slightly softening the horizon. The water remains mostly clear for viewing the cays.
Summer brings heavier rain showers and building clouds that can cast shadows over the shallow banks, dulling the water's color.
Tropical storms and heavy rain are most frequent, often churning up the sand and reducing water clarity. Overcast skies frequently mute the contrast between the ocean and the islands.
Storm risks fade and the skies begin to clear. The water settles, returning the sharp turquoise colors to the coastal views.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with the transition between the cloudy wet season and the clear dry season.
gemini.overview: Bali is known for its rice terraces, volcanic peaks and dramatic coastal cliffs. Visitors can walk the green terraces of Tegallalang or look out over the ocean from the limestone cliffs at Uluwatu. Inland, the volcanic cone of Mount Batur rises above a crater lake, with jungle waterfalls and river gorges nearby.

blurbs.text: Heavy rains and low clouds frequently obscure the volcanic peaks and coastal horizons. Trails around the crater lakes become muddy, and runoff can cloud the coastal waters, though the inland rice terraces remain bright green.
Rain showers and low cloud still hide the volcano peaks at times, though the rice terraces and forests are lush and bright green.
Skies are mostly clear, giving sharper views of the inland volcanoes and coastal drops. The forests and terraces are lush from the recent wet weather, making this a strong window for photography.

Clear, dry skies provide the sharpest visibility for sunrise hikes up Mount Batur and long views down the Uluwatu cliffs. The coastal waters appear bright blue against the limestone, and the jungle trails to inland waterfalls are firm and accessible.
The coastal cliffs offer clear sightlines over the water, though afternoon haze often softens the views of the inland valleys and crater lakes.
Cloud often builds over the central mountains and rain showers are back, though the coastal cliffs still give clear sightlines over the water.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the freezing and thawing of the lakes and the seasonal closure of high-elevation roads.
gemini.overview: The Canadian Rockies are made up of massive limestone peaks, deep valleys, and expansive icefields. Visitors drive the Icefields Parkway to see mountains and glaciers, or walk the shores of Moraine Lake and Lake Louise to view their bright turquoise waters. The scenery is at its most accessible, with the lakes thawed, from June through September.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the peaks and pine forests, and the famous lakes are frozen over. The road to Moraine Lake is closed to vehicles, but the Icefields Parkway stays open for winter driving past frozen waterfalls and glaciers.
Snow still covers the higher trails and viewpoints, and the major lakes are frozen. Melting snow in the lower valleys feeds the rivers and waterfalls.
Snow still blocks higher trails and viewpoints, and the major lakes often stay frozen into late May, but melting ice gives the rivers and waterfalls heavy flow.
The lake ice clears and the lakes take on the bright blue of glacial rock flour that makes Lake Louise and Moraine Lake famous, with high-elevation roads opening for driving.

The lakes are thawed and show the bright blue glacial rock flour that makes Lake Louise and Moraine Lake famous. High-elevation roads are open for driving, and the glaciers along the Icefields Parkway are clearly visible.
Snow dusts the mountains again, and the lakes are freezing. The access road to Moraine Lake typically closes to vehicles in the middle of the month as winter conditions set in.

gemini.depth_why: The river and temples stay the same, but heat, haze and the rains affect the views.
gemini.overview: The wide Chao Phraya River as it flows past the city's temples and high-rises is a defining Bangkok view. The signature sight is Wat Arun illuminated at night across the water. The surrounding landscape is a flat river plain.

blurbs.text: Cooler, drier air gives clear views of Wat Arun and the illuminated skyline from the Chao Phraya riverbanks at dusk, with ferries and longtail boats on the water.
Heat and haze soften the skyline, and the river views of Wat Arun are best at dusk, when ferries and longtail boats cross the water.
Afternoon downpours and heavy cloud come and go over the river, and clearer evenings still show Wat Arun and the illuminated skyline.

gemini.depth_why: The coastal scenery does not change across the months.
gemini.overview: Barbados is known for its coastal scenery, with a sharp contrast between its eastern and western shores. The Atlantic side features the rugged, rock-strewn beaches of Bathsheba, where heavy surf shapes the limestone formations. On the west coast, calmer waters meet flat stretches of sand.

blurbs.text: The Atlantic surf continually batters the eastern limestone rocks at Bathsheba, shaping the rugged shoreline. On the opposite side of the island, the western beaches offer flat stretches of sand and calm water.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise steadily toward a clear summer peak for coastal visibility, creating distinct seasonal groups.
gemini.overview: The Basque Country is known for its dramatic coastline, where green hills drop into the Bay of Biscay. The standout sights are the sweeping crescent of San Sebastián's La Concha bay and the jagged rock formations of the Flysch coast. Inland, modest forested mountains and traditional villages offer quieter rural views.

blurbs.text: Winter brings frequent rain and low clouds that obscure the coastal hills. The rough seas create dramatic waves against the Flysch cliffs, though shorter days limit time for coastal walks.
Bright green hillsides line the coast, and the lengthening days give ample time to drive the coastal roads and walk the cliff paths.
Clear skies and long daylight hours give the best visibility for the region's signature coastal views. The waters of La Concha bay appear bright blue against the surrounding green peaks.
Autumn brings more clouds and rain, softening the light over the coastal cliffs. The inland forests show muted fall colors, with heavier winter weather close behind.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise through spring to a summer peak, then fall through autumn to a winter low.
gemini.overview: Bavaria is known for the Bavarian Alps and the deep, clear lakes that sit below them. One signature view is Neuschwanstein Castle set against the mountains, while Lake Königssee has steep, fjord-like shores. Forests and rolling hills cover much of the region, with viewpoints accessible by cable car or mountain road. The scenery is best seen from late spring to early autumn, when high trails and passes are clear of snow.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the Alps and higher elevations, closing many mountain passes and high hiking trails. The lakes and lower valleys remain visible, often under a layer of snow, and cable cars run for winter sports, though daylight is short.
Snow still blankets the Alps, while the lower valleys show green meadows between the patches of snow. Waterfalls run high with meltwater, and the lower trails are walkable.
Green meadows fill the valleys while the higher peaks stay white. Waterfalls run high with meltwater, and lower trails are walkable.
Meadows and forests are green and most high Alpine passes are open to drivers, with some snow still on the peaks. Trails around Lake Königssee are clear.

The high Alpine passes, including the Rossfeld Panoramastrasse, are open to drivers. Trails around Lake Königssee and the viewpoints above Neuschwanstein Castle are clear, and the forests are deep green. Long daylight suits driving the scenic routes.
Autumn color peaks in the mixed forests of the lower Alps and around the lakes. Early snow can dust the highest peaks, though the high passes and cable cars generally still run.

gemini.depth_why: Scores vary by season, peaking in autumn when visibility is best and foliage turns, with lower scores in winter due to cold and haze.
gemini.overview: The primary scenic draw here is the Great Wall, which snakes across the rugged Yanshan mountains north of the city. Sections like Mutianyu and Jiankou offer sweeping views of the stone fortifications following the steep ridges and plunging into the valleys. Within the city, the vast scale of the Forbidden City and the hilltop pavilions of Jingshan Park provide striking urban vistas. The surrounding hills are heavily forested, turning vibrant colors in the autumn.

blurbs.text: Winter brings cold, dry air and occasional snow that dusts the mountains and the Great Wall. Haze and smog can sometimes obscure the longer views, but clear days give stark, leafless vistas of the rugged terrain.
The hills around the Great Wall are still mostly bare and brown, and spring winds can bring dust, though the mild days are good for walking the ridgelines.
Peach and apricot blossoms soften the rocky hillsides and the forests green up, though spring winds can bring dust.
The mountains are lush and fully green, providing a vibrant contrast to the stone of the Great Wall. Visibility is generally good before the heavier summer rains.
Summer is the wet season, bringing frequent rain and high humidity. The forests are at their thickest, but low clouds and summer haze can sometimes limit the sweeping views from the higher ridges.
Autumn brings the clearest skies and sharp views of the mountains and the city. The forests around the Great Wall are still green, and the clear air makes the hikes along the ridges rewarding.
The skies stay clear and the forests around the Great Wall turn bright shades of red and gold, making the hikes along the ridges particularly striking.
The autumn colors fade and the trees lose their leaves as the air turns sharply colder. Visibility is mostly clear before the winter haze settles in, with unobstructed views of the mountain contours.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with daylight and weather, peaking in summer when coastal views are clearest.
gemini.overview: Northern Ireland is known for its dramatic coastline, anchored by the Giant's Causeway and its thousands of interlocking basalt columns. The Causeway Coastal Route traces the edge of the country, passing sea cliffs, ruined castles and sweeping glens. Inland, the landscape softens into rolling green hills and quiet forests, including the tunnel of beech trees known as the Dark Hedges. In the south-east, the granite Mourne Mountains rise above the Irish Sea, with Slieve Donard at about 2,800 feet.

blurbs.text: Short days and frequent rain limit time for coastal drives and walks. The Giant's Causeway and the Dark Hedges are quiet, but low clouds and storms often obscure the sea views along the northern cliffs.
Longer days give more time for driving the Causeway Coastal Route, and the glens and hills are bright green, though rain and wind are still common along the exposed coast.

Long summer days provide the best conditions for exploring the coast. The basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway and the sea cliffs are clearest, and the extended twilight allows for late-evening drives along the northern shore.
Autumn colors show in the inland glens and the Dark Hedges. The coast is open to drivers and walkers, but daylight is shortening and Atlantic storms roll in.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility for aerial views and access to forest roads change with the wet and dry seasons.
gemini.overview: The primary scenic draw is the coastline, defined by the barrier reef cayes and the deep marine sinkhole of the Great Blue Hole seen from the air. Inland, the landscape transitions to dense tropical forests and modest mountain ridges. Clear skies and calm waters from late winter through spring provide the best visibility for aerial flights and boat trips.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and calm waters maximize visibility for aerial views over the Great Blue Hole and boat rides along the barrier reef. Inland forest roads are dry and easy to navigate.
Clouds and rain showers can obscure aerial views of the reef. The inland forests are lush and green, though some unpaved routes turn muddy.

Heavy rains and frequent storms churn up coastal waters, reducing the striking color contrasts of the marine sinkholes. Low cloud cover often blocks scenic flights, and dirt roads into the forest reserves flood.
Rains begin to taper off, slowly restoring water clarity around the cayes. Aerial flights over the reef resume more regular schedules as the heavy cloud cover breaks.

gemini.depth_why: Access to the high-elevation rim and scenic byways changes distinctly with the heavy winter snowpack and summer melting.
gemini.overview: The deep blue caldera of Crater Lake and the volcanic peaks of the Cascades define the scenery of this region. Visitors can drive through ancient lava fields, pine forests, and river canyons around Bend. Crater Lake's high-elevation rim road is open only during the short summer season.

blurbs.text: Heavy snow keeps the North Entrance and Rim Drive at Crater Lake shut, as well as the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway. Views of the caldera are limited to the South Entrance, and winter storms frequently obscure the mountains.
Plowing begins on the high-elevation roads, but the Rim Drive and Cascade Lakes routes remain closed by deep snowpack. Lower-elevation lava fields and river canyons around Bend are clear.

The snowpack recedes enough for the North Entrance and parts of the Rim Drive to open. High-elevation trails may still hold snow, but the main viewpoints over the caldera and the Cascade peaks are accessible.
The full Rim Drive around Crater Lake and the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway are open. Visitors can drive to high viewpoints and hike the volcanic trails without snow blocking the paths.
Early snow dusts the Cascade peaks. The main scenic drives usually stay open through the first half of the month, though sudden storms can temporarily shut high-elevation roads.

gemini.depth_why: The avenues and river stay the same, but the parks are bare and gray in winter and green in the warm months.
gemini.overview: The Brandenburg Gate and the embankments of the Spree River are signature views of the German capital. The wide riverways and extensive city parks create pleasant vistas across the flat urban terrain.

blurbs.text: Bare trees and gray skies leave the parks and the Spree embankments muted, though the Brandenburg Gate and the broad avenues still show clearly.
Green parks and long daylight make the Tiergarten and the paved paths along the Spree pleasant, with the Brandenburg Gate at the end of the broad avenues.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the summer monsoon when clouds obscure the mountains, and peak in spring and autumn.
gemini.overview: Bhutan is known for the Himalayas, with deep valleys, dense forests and high passes. The signature view is the Tiger's Nest monastery clinging to a cliffside, while the Punakha Dzong sits at the confluence of two rivers. The scenery is best seen in spring and autumn, when the skies are clear and the mountain views are unobstructed.

blurbs.text: Winter brings clear skies and sharp views of the high peaks, though snow can close the higher passes like Dochula. The valleys are cold but accessible.
Spring is a prime time for mountain views ahead of the monsoon. The valleys are green, and the high passes are clear of winter snow.
The summer monsoon brings heavy rain and low clouds that often hide the high peaks. Landslides can occasionally block mountain roads.
The monsoon rains begin to ease, and the clouds start to lift, revealing the mountains again. The forests and valleys are lush from the summer rain.
Autumn offers the clearest skies of the year, with sharp, unobstructed views of the Himalayas. The weather is dry, making it the best time for the high passes and viewpoints.
Early winter keeps the skies clear for mountain viewing, though temperatures drop and snow begins to accumulate on the highest routes.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery and access to it remain consistent throughout the year.
gemini.overview: The Big Island is known for its active geology, with the active caldera of Kilauea and the high summit of Mauna Kea dominating the interior. The coasts range from the dry, lava-strewn Kona and Kohala sides to the lush Hamakua coast, known for deep valleys and tall waterfalls.

blurbs.text: The volcanic landscapes of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park and the high-altitude views from Mauna Kea are accessible. The Hamakua coast offers views of Akaka Falls and Waipio Valley, while the western coasts show stark contrasts between black lava fields and the ocean.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise in spring, peak in summer, and fall in autumn and winter as snow and cold limit access.
gemini.overview: The Black Forest is known for its dense, dark evergreen woods, rolling hills, and deep valleys. Wooded ridges, half-timbered villages, and the multi-tiered Triberg waterfalls fill the landscape. The best views are found along the Schwarzwaldhochstraße (Black Forest High Road), which offers sweeping panoramas over the Rhine plain.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the higher elevations, transforming the dark woods into a winter landscape. Some minor roads and trails may be difficult to navigate, but the main routes are usually clear. The Triberg waterfalls often freeze into ice formations.
Snow lingers on the highest ridges while the valleys and lower hills thaw, and the waterfalls run heavy with spring runoff.
The forests are dense and green, and the weather is warm enough for long drives and walks. The Schwarzwaldhochstraße gives clear views over the valleys and the Rhine plain.
The forests are at their deepest green and the days are warm and long. The Schwarzwaldhochstraße gives clear views over the Rhine plain, and the trails around the Triberg waterfalls are easy to walk.
The forests are still dense and green, with crisp mornings and clear views along the Schwarzwaldhochstraße and around the Triberg waterfalls.

Autumn brings color to the deciduous trees mixed among the evergreens, creating a contrast against the dark pines. The air is crisp, and visibility from the high roads is often excellent before the winter snows begin.

gemini.depth_why: The vineyards change from bare winter branches to full summer green and autumn colors.
gemini.overview: The primary views are the flat, elegant urban riverfront and the surrounding vine-covered estates of the Médoc. The Place de la Bourse reflects in a massive water mirror, creating a striking symmetrical view of the 18th-century facades. Beyond the city limits, the landscape transitions into orderly rows of vineyards stretching across gentle slopes.

blurbs.text: The vines are bare and pruned back for the winter, leaving the vineyard slopes stark and quiet. The city's riverfront architecture is the main visual draw.
Buds are breaking on the vines and the slopes turn green again. The city's riverfront architecture remains the main visual draw.
The vineyards of the Médoc are in full green leaf, and the water mirror at the Place de la Bourse reflects the grand architecture along the Garonne river.
The vine leaves turn gold and red across the Médoc, and the water mirror at the Place de la Bourse still reflects the grand architecture along the Garonne river.
The last gold and red vine leaves hang on across the Médoc before the vines go bare. The city's riverfront architecture is the main visual draw.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with the monsoon rains, which affect visibility and access to the rainforests and mountains.
gemini.overview: Malaysian Borneo is known for its ancient rainforests and the granite peaks of Mount Kinabalu. The primary draws are the dense, towering canopy of the Danum Valley and the winding Kinabatangan River, where boat trips reveal the jungle banks. The scenery is best viewed during the drier months, when forest trails are clear.

blurbs.text: Heavy monsoon rains often obscure the views and swell the rivers. Trails in the rainforests can be muddy and difficult to navigate, and the peaks of Mount Kinabalu are frequently hidden by thick clouds.
Rain showers are fewer and the rivers run lower. The rainforest canopy is easier to explore, and Mount Kinabalu shows itself more often.

The drier weather brings the clearest views of Mount Kinabalu's granite summit. The trails through the Danum Valley are at their most accessible, and boat trips along the Kinabatangan River offer unobstructed views of the dense jungle banks.
Rain showers become more frequent as the wet season approaches. The rainforest remains lush and green, though low clouds may begin to gather around the higher elevations.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise as the floodwaters arrive and peak in the dry winter months, then fall as the waters recede and the rains return.
gemini.overview: The Okavango Delta is an inland river system that spills into the Kalahari Desert, creating a vast network of channels, lagoons, and islands. The flooded landscapes are best appreciated from a traditional mokoro canoe gliding through the reeds, or from a small plane above the floodplains. The landscape changes with the annual flood, which peaks from June to September.

blurbs.text: The rains bring thick vegetation, but the main floodwaters have not yet arrived. Water levels in the channels are lower, and some areas may be less accessible by boat, though the landscape is green and lush.
The rains have ended, and floodwater from the Angolan highlands is on its way. The channels are still low and the plains are green.
Floodwater from the Angolan highlands is filling the channels, widening the waterways across the dry plains.

The floodwaters reach their highest levels, creating the classic delta scenery of deep channels, lily-covered lagoons, and flooded plains. This is the prime time to explore the waterways by mokoro or boat, with clear skies and dry weather.
Water levels have dropped and the landscape is dry, with shrunken channels and lagoons.
The first rains of the year bring new growth to the plains, while the channels stay low.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility and daylight hours change with the seasons, affecting the views from the hills.
gemini.overview: Budapest is known for the wide Danube River dividing the flat Pest side from the steep Buda Hills. The signature view looks across the water to the Parliament building and the Chain Bridge. Viewpoints like Gellért Hill and the Fisherman's Bastion provide sweeping panoramas of the river basin.

blurbs.text: Winter brings early sunsets and occasional fog that can obscure the river basin from higher vantage points.
Visibility is improving as the winter haze thins, opening the view from the Buda Hills across the river.
Long daylight hours provide ample time to walk the riverbanks and take in the panoramas from Gellért Hill.
Autumn brings clear skies and changing colors to the trees lining the Danube and the slopes of Buda.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery is accessible and visible year-round with no significant seasonal changes.
gemini.overview: The Canary Islands are known for dramatic volcanic landscapes, from the towering peak of Mount Teide to the shifting sand dunes of Fuerteventura. Visitors can drive through the ancient laurel forests of the Anaga mountains or hike among the striking rock formations of the Roques de García. The coasts have steep cliffs and black sand beaches.

blurbs.text: Clear days give expansive views from Mount Teide and the Anaga mountains. The volcanic peaks, coastal cliffs and ancient forests vary from island to island, and the dunes of Fuerteventura make a striking contrast to the ocean.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise and fall with the seasons, reflecting the appeal of the coastal scenery in warmer months versus the starker, colder winter.
gemini.overview: The draw here is the classic New England coastline, with long sandy beaches, dunes, and historic maritime villages. Especially scenic are the sweeping dunes around Provincetown and the gray-shingled towns of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. The views are best appreciated in the warmer months when the weather is clear and the ferries run frequently.

blurbs.text: Winter brings a stark, quiet beauty to the coast. The beaches and dunes are empty, and the gray-shingled villages look especially austere against the winter sky, though cold winds make long walks less appealing.
The dunes and beaches are quiet, offering peaceful views of the shoreline before the summer crowds, though the water and wind are still chilly.
Bright coastal light and warming weather bring out the dunes around Provincetown and the island villages, and ferries to Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard run regular schedules.

The coastal scenery is at its most classic. The long sandy beaches, sweeping dunes, and historic maritime villages are bathed in summer sun, making for ideal conditions to explore the shoreline and the islands.
Crisp air gives quieter coastal views. The beaches are mostly empty, and the dunes take on a softer light, with peaceful scenery as the busy season fades.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility and access change with the dry summer and wet winter seasons.
gemini.overview: The dramatic meeting of steep mountains and the Atlantic Ocean defines the scenery of the Cape Peninsula. Table Mountain rises directly above the city bowl, offering views of the coastline and surrounding peaks from its flat summit. Farther south, the cliffs of Cape Point and Chapman's Peak Drive provide miles of ocean views.

blurbs.text: Dry, clear days give the best visibility from the peaks and coastal roads. Strong southeasterly winds occasionally push a thick layer of cloud over Table Mountain, which can obscure the summit and halt the cableway.
The strong southeasterly winds are fading, leaving calmer air for coastal drives. Rain showers and low clouds become more frequent, occasionally blocking the views from higher elevations.

Storms bring heavy rain and thick fog that frequently hide the mountains and coastline. Clear days between the fronts provide sharp views, but the cableway and mountain trails often shut in poor weather.
The rains are lighter and sightlines down the peninsula are long and clear, though lingering cold fronts can still bring sudden cloud cover to the peaks.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with snow cover, trail access, and glacier visibility across the seasons.
gemini.overview: The Mont Blanc massif dominates the Chamonix valley, offering some of the most dramatic alpine scenery in the world. The Aiguille du Midi cable car provides a close-up view of the peaks and the Mer de Glace glacier. Summer opens the high hiking trails and mountain passes, while winter covers the landscape in deep snow for skiing and snowshoeing.

blurbs.text: Deep snow covers the valley and the peaks. The Aiguille du Midi cable car runs, giving clear, freezing views of the Mont Blanc massif, though high hiking trails and some mountain passes are closed for the winter.
Snow lingers on the valley floor and the high peaks stay white, while trails at lower elevations are clearing. High-altitude routes and passes are still blocked by snow.

The high alpine trails are clear of snow, giving the full range of viewpoints across the Mont Blanc massif. The Mer de Glace is easy to reach, and the long days allow for extensive drives and walks through the valleys and over the passes.

Autumn brings changing colors to the lower forests. The high peaks may see early dustings of snow, and while some high trails begin to close, the Aiguille du Midi still carries visitors to the main viewpoints.

The transition to winter brings early snows and shorter days. Many high trails are closed, and the landscape is caught between autumn bareness and winter snow cover, though the main peaks are still visible.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the agricultural cycle of the vineyards, from bare winter branches to lush summer green and golden autumn foliage.
gemini.overview: The region's visual appeal centers on its rolling, vine-covered hillsides that stretch across the Marne valley and the Montagne de Reims. Historic villages and the distant spires of the Reims Cathedral provide a classic rural French backdrop to the agricultural landscape. The scenery peaks during the autumn harvest when the vineyards turn vibrant shades of gold and red.

blurbs.text: Winter leaves the vineyards bare and the hillsides stark, with frequent gray skies and occasional frost covering the fields.
Spring brings bud break to the vines, adding faint green hues to the rolling hills and valleys.
The vineyards fill out into lush, dense green canopies that blanket the slopes of the Montagne de Reims.
The autumn harvest transforms the landscape as the vine leaves turn brilliant shades of yellow, gold, and deep red.
The bright autumn foliage drops quickly, leaving the hillsides mostly bare as the first winter chills set in.

gemini.depth_why: The landscape is visible year-round, with marsh grasses changing from green to brown in the winter.
gemini.overview: The coastal Lowcountry is known for flat, tidal salt marshes and maritime forests of live oaks draped in Spanish moss. The urban centers feature historic waterfronts, such as Charleston's pastel Rainbow Row, and Savannah's shaded, park-like squares. The views are best seen from coastal drives or by walking the historic districts.

blurbs.text: The tidal marsh grasses turn a golden brown. The evergreen live oaks and their Spanish moss keep the maritime forests and city squares shaded, though deciduous trees lose their leaves.
The salt marshes are bright green and the maritime forests are dense. The evergreen live oaks provide heavy shade over the city squares and coastal roads.

gemini.depth_why: Visibility changes drastically with the dry season smoke and the monsoon rains.
gemini.overview: The forested mountains and river valleys of Northern Thailand provide a lush backdrop to the region's ancient temples and rural villages. The peaks of Doi Inthanon offer sweeping views over the surrounding highlands, while dense jungles hide tiered waterfalls and winding mountain passes. The clearest views come in the cooler, dry months before the agricultural burning season begins.

blurbs.text: Clear skies reveal the full depth of the mountain ranges and valleys. The air is cool, making drives up to Doi Inthanon and walks to the region's waterfalls comfortable, with sharp visibility across the forested highlands.
Haze begins to build in the valleys as the dry weather continues. The mountain outlines soften, though the higher viewpoints still give sweeping sights over the jungle canopy.

Heavy smoke from agricultural burning fills the air, severely reducing visibility. The mountain views are largely obscured by a thick haze, and the scenery is mostly limited to the immediate surroundings.
The first rains begin to clear the lingering smoke from the air. Visibility improves, though low clouds often hang over the peaks and the waterfalls are just starting to regain their flow.

Frequent monsoon rains turn the forests a deep, vibrant green and fill the rivers and waterfalls to their peaks. Heavy cloud cover often hides the highest viewpoints, and some unpaved rural roads become difficult to navigate.
The rains taper off, leaving the jungles lush and the waterfalls flowing heavily. The skies clear, bringing back sharp views of the mountain ridges and valleys.

gemini.depth_why: The dry and wet seasons dictate water clarity and visibility, creating distinct periods for viewing the landscapes.
gemini.overview: Chiapas is known for its dense forests, deep canyons, and a network of rivers and waterfalls. The Cañón del Sumidero cuts through the terrain with vertical walls rising thousands of feet above the water. The cascades of Agua Azul flow in wide tiers through the jungle, and the Maya temples of Palenque rise out of the rainforest. The colonial architecture of San Cristóbal de las Casas adds a historic draw to the lush landscape.

blurbs.text: The dry season keeps the rivers and waterfalls running clear, showing off the bright turquoise color at Agua Azul. Forest trails are mostly dry, and the canyon viewpoints offer clear lines of sight.
The first rains begin to swell the rivers, increasing the flow over the cascades. The water color starts to shift from blue to green as runoff enters the streams.
Heavy summer rains turn the rivers and waterfalls muddy and brown, hiding the famous blue tones. Low clouds and fog frequently settle into the highland valleys and obscure the canyon rims.
The rains taper off and the rivers begin to settle. The water slowly clears, returning to its lighter shades, and the forests are thick and green from the wet season.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with the distinct seasons, from clear summer access to wet, cloudy winters.
gemini.overview: The Chilean Lake District is known for the snow-capped cones of the Osorno and Villarrica volcanoes rising directly above deep, glacially carved lakes. Ancient lenga and araucaria forests cover the lower slopes, cut by fast-flowing rivers and waterfalls. The clearest views and most walkable trails run from November through March.

blurbs.text: The skies are at their clearest for viewing the Osorno and Villarrica volcanoes. High-elevation trails in Huerquehue National Park are free of snow, allowing hikers to reach the alpine lakes and ancient araucaria and lenga forests.
The lenga forests turn deep red and orange, contrasting with the evergreen araucaria trees and the blue lakes. Clouds gather more often around the volcano peaks, and rain showers are more frequent.
Heavy rain and low clouds often obscure the volcanoes. Lower-elevation walks to waterfalls like Petrohué are still possible, though higher trails are muddy and see their first snows.

Heavy rain falls in the valleys and deep snow on the mountains. Many trails in the national parks are shut, and persistent cloud cover hides the signature volcano views, though the snow-covered peaks look dramatic on rare clear days.
Snowmelt swells the rivers, making the Petrohué Waterfalls and other cascades particularly powerful. Rain and fog are still common, but the lower valleys are bright green as the weather warms.
The snow line retreats up the volcanoes, opening up more hiking routes through the forests. Skies clear more often, revealing the classic views of the peaks mirrored in the lakes below.

gemini.depth_why: The landscape changes with the snow, the sea ice, the summer wildflowers and the fall color.
gemini.overview: Churchill sits at the edge of the subarctic tundra and the rocky shores of Hudson Bay. The tundra is white and frozen through winter, bright with wildflowers such as fireweed in midsummer, red and gold in early fall, and brown and gray in between. Hudson Bay is open water in summer and sea ice in winter.

blurbs.text: Snow covers the tundra and the thin forest edge, and the low sun gives short, soft light. The landscape is white and quiet, with little color beyond blue shadows on the snow.
Longer days bring bright light to the snow-covered tundra, and sea ice stretches across Hudson Bay under clear skies.
The snow is thin and patchy, leaving the tundra gray and brown while Hudson Bay is still covered in ice.
Melting snow turns the ground to mud, and broken ice drifts along the shore of the bay, leaving a drab, gray landscape.
The ice breaks up on Hudson Bay, and the first green and early wildflowers spread across the tundra.
The tundra is green and covered in wildflowers such as fireweed, and Hudson Bay is open water along the rocky shore and the Churchill River estuary.
The tundra turns red, orange and gold, and Hudson Bay is still open water along the shore.
Snow comes and goes across the brown and gray tundra, and ice forms along the shore of Hudson Bay.

gemini.depth_why: Scores follow the dry and wet seasons of the Andes.
gemini.overview: The Colombian Andes are known for steep, green mountainsides and the high-altitude cloud forests that cover them. The signature view is the Cocora Valley, where the world's tallest wax palms rise from misty pastures. The coffee region adds rolling hills dotted with traditional villages, while higher elevations hold paramo ecosystems and scattered glaciers.

blurbs.text: The first dry season brings the clearest skies to the mountains. The trails through the Cocora Valley and the high paramo are mostly dry, making it easier to reach viewpoints and see the wax palms against blue skies.

The first wet season brings frequent rain and heavy cloud cover to the mountains. The cloud forests live up to their name, often shrouded in mist that obscures the longer views across the valleys, and trails can become deeply muddy.
A second dry season brings clearer air. The green hills of the coffee region and the high peaks are visible, and the dirt roads connecting the mountain villages are easier to navigate.

The second wet season is typically the rainiest time in the Andes. Low clouds and fog frequently block the views of the peaks and valleys, and heavy rains can cause landslides that temporarily close mountain roads.
The rains begin to taper off as the year ends. The valleys are lush and green from the wet season, and the clouds start to lift, revealing more of the mountain scenery.

gemini.depth_why: The year divides into a clear dry season with optimal coastal views and a wetter season with reduced visibility.
gemini.overview: The Colombian Caribbean is known for the boulder-strewn coast of Tayrona National Park, where jungle-covered hills meet golden beaches and huge granite boulders. Cartagena's walled old town, with its colorful colonial buildings, sits on the same coast. Inland, the landscape shifts to dense mangroves and coastal forests.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and calm seas make this the best weather for the coastal scenery, from the boulder beaches of Tayrona to the sea walls of Cartagena.
Passing rain showers become more frequent, occasionally clouding the water and softening the coastal views, though mornings often remain clear.
Heavy rains and overcast skies can obscure the horizon, and the trails through Tayrona's jungle turn muddy.

gemini.depth_why: The harbor stays the same, but the days are short and gray in winter and long and bright in the warm months.
gemini.overview: Copenhagen is built on flat coastal islands, and its most recognizable views are along the waterfront. The signature sight is Nyhavn, a harbor lined with brightly painted townhouses and wooden boats.

blurbs.text: Short, gray days leave the harbor muted, though the painted townhouses of Nyhavn and the canals still show well in low light.
Long, bright days and green parks light up the painted townhouses and wooden boats of Nyhavn and the historic canals along the waterfront.

gemini.depth_why: The scores rise through spring to a summer peak and fall through autumn, driven by daylight and weather on the coast path.
gemini.overview: Cornwall is known for its rugged coastline, where high cliffs drop into the Atlantic and sandy coves sit between rocky headlands. The South West Coast Path traces the entire edge, passing landmarks like Land's End and the tidal island of St Michael's Mount. Inland, the scenery shifts to rolling farmland and quiet villages. The views are clearest and easiest to reach from late spring through summer.

blurbs.text: Winter brings short days, frequent rain and strong winds off the Atlantic. The coast path is often muddy and exposed, and low light limits the views of the cliffs and coves. St Michael's Mount and the headlands look dramatic in rough weather, but access is harder.
Longer days and drier trails make the coast path easier to walk, and the views of the cliffs and the sea open up as the weather settles. The headlands and coves are quiet before the summer crowds.

Long days and warmer weather make this the best time to see the coast. The South West Coast Path gives clear views of Land's End, St Ives harbor and the rocky shoreline. The sea and sky are at their brightest, though the main viewpoints get busy.

Autumn brings shorter days and a return to wetter, windier weather. The coast path is still walkable, but the views are often softened by mist or rain. The crowds thin out, leaving the cliffs and beaches quieter.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the wet season when clouds and rain obscure views and make trails muddy.
gemini.overview: Costa Rica is known for its dense cloud forests, active volcanoes, waterfalls, and tropical coastlines. Signature views include the perfect cone of Arenal Volcano rising above the jungle and the beaches of Manuel Antonio National Park against the lush rainforest.

blurbs.text: The dry season brings clear skies, making this the best time to see the peak of Arenal Volcano and the sweeping coastal views at Manuel Antonio. Trails through the cloud forests and down to waterfalls are mostly dry and accessible.
The transition to the wet season begins. Clouds start to gather around the volcanic peaks and afternoon showers become common, but mornings usually give clear views of the coasts and forests.
Rain is frequent, swelling the rivers and waterfalls to their most powerful flows. The forests are lush and green, though low clouds often hide the higher mountain peaks and volcanoes.

Heavy rains define the peak of the wet season. Trails can be muddy or washed out, and thick clouds frequently obscure the volcanoes and coastal viewpoints. Waterfalls are dramatic, but reaching them can be difficult.

The rains begin to ease, and the landscapes are exceptionally green from the wet season. Cloud cover starts to lift, revealing the mountains and volcanoes more often, though trails may still be muddy.
The dry season returns, clearing the skies and drying out the trails. The forests remain lush from the recent rains, and views of the coastlines and volcanic peaks are clear.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise slightly in the warmer, greener months and fall in the colder, barer winter.
gemini.overview: The Cotswolds are known for rolling hills, quiet woodlands, and honey-colored stone villages. The landscape is rural, with narrow lanes connecting small settlements set against green pastures and low ridges. The most famous views are the villages such as Bibury and Castle Combe, which blend seamlessly into the surrounding countryside.

blurbs.text: The hills and woodlands are bare, and the landscape takes on a muted, quiet tone. The stone villages stand out sharply against the winter fields, though short days limit the time for walking the rural lanes.
New green fills the pastures and woodlands and the rolling hills brighten, and the longer days make it easier to explore the viewpoints and village settings.
The rural scenery is at its greenest and most vibrant. The gentle hills, woodlands, and pastures are fully leafed out, providing a lush backdrop for the honey-stone villages.
The green pastures fade as the woodlands take on autumn colors, adding warmth to the landscape around the stone villages before the trees drop their leaves.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise from winter lows to a summer peak as access to islands and coastal viewpoints improves.
gemini.overview: The Dalmatian Coast is known for its dramatic meeting of mountains and the Adriatic Sea, with steep limestone cliffs dropping into clear water. Hundreds of islands dot the coastline, with quiet coves and pine-forested shores. Signature views include the walled city of Dubrovnik rising directly from the coast and the terraced waterfalls of Krka and Plitvice Lakes.

blurbs.text: Winter brings quiet to the coast, with rougher seas and fewer ferries running to the islands. The coastal mountains and walled cities remain striking, though inland waterfalls like Plitvice may be partially frozen or surrounded by snow, and some trails close for safety.

Rising water levels in the inland rivers make the waterfalls at Krka and Plitvice particularly powerful. Coastal drives give clear views of the islands, and ferry schedules are widening as the weather warms.

The coastal scenery is at its best, with calm, clear waters highlighting the limestone cliffs and island archipelagos. Full ferry schedules allow easy access to remote island viewpoints, and the long days provide ample time for coastal drives and walking the walls of Dubrovnik.

Autumn colors begin to appear in the forests around the inland lakes and waterfalls. The coastal views remain clear, though ferry services to the smaller islands start to reduce as the season winds down.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery does not change, but extreme summer heat limits how much of it can be seen comfortably.
gemini.overview: Death Valley is one of the world's premier desert landscapes, defined by vast salt flats, painted canyons, and towering dunes. The scenery is stark and expansive, with viewpoints looking out over the lowest point in North America.

blurbs.text: Cool, clear days make it comfortable to walk out onto the white salt flats of Badwater Basin, and the light is sharp on the eroded badlands at Zabriskie Point and the rippled Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes.
Highs reach the 90s, but the salt flats, badlands and dunes are still comfortable to see in the early morning and evening.
Heat above 100 degrees Fahrenheit limits most visits to short stops at the viewpoints and walks at dawn and dusk.
Daytime highs often above 110 degrees Fahrenheit limit viewing to short roadside stops and the cooler hours around sunrise. The salt flats and dunes are best seen at first light.
Afternoons are still very hot, so the salt flats and dunes are best seen in the morning and at sunset.
Pleasant temperatures and clear air give sharp views across the salt flats to the Panamint Range.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise as the park road opens and snow clears, peaking in summer, then fall as winter closes access.
gemini.overview: The Alaska Range dominates the Interior, anchored by Denali, the highest peak in North America. Visitors come for the vast tundra, braided rivers, and glaciers that shape the valleys. The signature view is Denali itself, often seen from Wonder Lake or on a flightseeing trip, though the mountain creates its own weather and is frequently hidden by clouds.

blurbs.text: Deep snow and extreme cold limit access to the Interior. The Denali Park Road is mostly closed to vehicles, and daylight is brief, leaving only a few hours to see the snow-covered peaks.

Days lengthen significantly, bringing more light to the snow-covered Alaska Range. The park road stays closed to most traffic, but flightseeing gives views of the glaciers and peaks while the snow still lies deep.
The snow begins to melt, and the lower sections of the Denali Park Road open to vehicles. The tundra is still brown, but the rivers start to flow freely as the ice breaks up.

The park road is open as far as conditions allow, providing access to the deep Interior and viewpoints like Wonder Lake. The tundra is green, and long daylight hours give ample time to watch for the clouds to part around Denali.

The tundra turns bright red and gold, creating a striking contrast against the first dustings of new snow on the peaks. The park road begins to close as the month progresses and winter weather returns.
Snow covers the landscape again, and the park road closes to most vehicles. The views are stark and white, with shortening days limiting the time to see the mountains.

gemini.depth_why: Scores rise from winter lows to a peak in the autumn harvest season.
gemini.overview: The Douro Valley is known for its steep, terraced vineyards rising directly from the Douro River. The scenery is best seen from the water or the winding roads that trace the valley walls. Porto anchors the region with its own riverfront views, where the city's historic center steps down to the water.

blurbs.text: Winter brings bare vines and cooler, often damp weather. The river and the terraced hills remain visible, with the bare terraces standing out in the winter light.
Spring brings green growth back to the terraced vineyards. The weather warms, making boat trips on the river and drives along the valley roads more comfortable.
The vines are fully green and the valley is warm and bright. The steep terraces stand out clearly against the river, and viewpoints along the winding roads offer long sights down the valley.
Autumn turns the terraced vineyards red, gold, and yellow. The colors stand out sharply against the river and the steep valley walls, making this the most striking time to see the landscape.
The autumn color fades and the vines go bare as winter approaches. The valley is quieter, and the views rest on the shape of the terraces and the river itself.

gemini.depth_why: The skyline and dunes stay the same, but summer heat and humidity make it hard to enjoy them outdoors.
gemini.overview: Dubai is known for the sharp contrast between its futuristic skyline and the surrounding desert. The signature view is the Burj Khalifa and the dense cluster of skyscrapers rising from the flat coastal plain. Beyond the city limits, the landscape shifts immediately to rolling sand dunes, which can be seen on drives into the desert.

blurbs.text: Mild, clear days with highs from the upper 70s to the mid 80s Fahrenheit make it comfortable to take in the skyline from the Burj Khalifa and to drive out to the dunes.
Highs reach the 90s, so the skyline and the dunes are best seen early or late in the day.
Highs in the upper 90s to over 100 degrees Fahrenheit shorten daytime outings, and the dunes and skyline are best seen around sunrise and sunset.
Highs above 100 degrees Fahrenheit and heavy humidity make it hard to spend time outdoors, so views come mostly from air-conditioned observation decks, and haze often softens the skyline.
Midday heat is still strong, but evenings are comfortable enough for skyline views and drives out to the dunes.

gemini.depth_why: The year divides into a clear dry season, a wet season, and a transitional period with a short dry spell.
gemini.overview: The Ecuadorian Andes are known for the Avenue of the Volcanoes, a high-altitude corridor of glaciated peaks and deep valleys. The terrain shifts from the perfect cone of Cotopaxi and the massive slopes of Chimborazo to the steep-sided crater lake of Laguna Quilotoa. Lower down, the eastern and western slopes of the Andes are carpeted with lush cloud forests full of ferns and orchids.

blurbs.text: The dry season brings the clearest skies to the highlands, revealing the snow-capped summits of Cotopaxi and Chimborazo. High winds sweep across the paramo, but with little heavy rain the trails to the Quilotoa crater and the high mountain passes stay firmly packed.

Clouds gather around the high peaks, and afternoon rain showers are frequent across the valleys. A short dry spell often comes around the turn of the year, giving brief windows of clear morning visibility for the major volcanoes.

Heavy cloud cover frequently obscures the highest glaciated peaks, and persistent rain softens the trails and rural dirt roads. The lower cloud forests and paramo grasslands turn deep green, though visitors must rely on early mornings for a chance to see the volcanic cones.

gemini.depth_why: Scores dip in winter due to short daylight and frequent low clouds obscuring the views.
gemini.overview: Edinburgh's dramatic topography is built across a series of extinct volcanoes and rocky crags. The primary natural draws are Arthur's Seat and the Salisbury Crags, which rise sharply above the streets and offer sweeping views of the skyline and the distant Firth of Forth.

blurbs.text: Short daylight hours and frequent low clouds or fog can obscure the wider views from the summits, and winter weather often makes the steep paths up the crags slippery.
Long daylight hours allow for late evening walks up Arthur's Seat and the Salisbury Crags, with clear views over the city and the water.

gemini.depth_why: The landscape stays the same, but summer heat and spring dust affect the views.
gemini.overview: The region is known for the stark contrast between the Sahara's arid expanses and the lush, palm-lined banks of the Nile. Visitors look for the silhouettes of the Giza pyramids against the desert sky and the rugged mountains meeting the Red Sea coast.

blurbs.text: Dry, clear air and mild days give unobstructed views of the Nile Valley, the Giza pyramids and the Red Sea coast.
Dust-laden spring winds sometimes soften the horizon, but the dunes, riverbanks and ancient monuments are still prominent.
Rising heat and occasional dust haze soften the horizon, and the best views come in the early morning and at sunset.
Daytime highs often above 105 degrees Fahrenheit limit viewing to the early morning and the hours around sunset, and haze softens the long views over the Nile and the desert.
Heat is still strong at midday, but the evenings are comfortable for views of the Nile and the pyramids.

gemini.depth_why: Scores form clear seasonal stages based on snow cover, trail access, and daylight.
gemini.overview: The region is known for the sheer granite spires of Mount Fitz Roy and its neighbor Cerro Torre rising sharply above the Patagonian steppe. Massive ice fields feed into the surrounding lakes, most notably the towering blue wall of the Perito Moreno Glacier. The valleys hold dense lenga forests and glacial rivers that are best viewed during the long days from November to March.

blurbs.text: Long daylight hours give plenty of time on the mountain trails and at the glacier viewpoints. The granite peaks are mostly clear of snow, and the ice fields are highly active.
The lenga forests below the peaks turn red and orange. Daylight is shortening, but the main viewpoints and valleys are easy to reach.
Snow accumulates on the higher trails, limiting access to some mountain viewpoints.
Short days and deep snow shut many high-elevation paths. The main glacier walkways stay open, offering views of the ice against a snow-covered landscape.
Snow still blocks many of the higher trekking routes, though the ice fields and mountain bases are easier to reach as the days lengthen.
Snowmelt is clearing the higher trekking routes, and the ice fields and mountain bases are easy to reach as the days lengthen.

gemini.depth_why: Scores drop during the rainy season when roads and trails become difficult.
gemini.overview: Ethiopia is known for its dramatic highlands, deep valleys, and ancient rock-hewn settlements. The Simien Mountains offer sheer cliffs and deep gorges, while the Danakil Depression provides a stark, volcanic desert landscape. The rock churches of Lalibela blend human history with the rugged terrain. The best views are found during the dry season when skies are clear and remote roads are passable.

blurbs.text: Clear skies and dry trails make this the best time to see the Simien Mountains and the Danakil Depression. The landscapes are vivid, and remote routes are fully passable.
The short rains bring some clouds and occasional showers. The highlands are greener, though some dirt roads may be muddy and visibility can occasionally drop.

Heavy rains dominate the highlands and cloud often covers the mountain views, though the countryside is a vivid green and the waterfalls run full. Many unpaved roads and trails in the Simien Mountains turn slow going.
The heavy rains taper off, leaving the highlands lush and green. Waterfalls are at their peak flow, though some roads may still be recovering from the wet season.

gemini.depth_why: The scenery changes with the distinct wet and dry seasons, which alter water levels, reflections, and trail access.
gemini.overview: The Everglades is known for its vast, flat expanses of sawgrass prairies and dense mangrove forests. Visitors view these wetland landscapes from raised boardwalks, kayaks navigating coastal waterways, and airboats crossing the shallow marshes. The scenery is clearest and most accessible during the dry winter months.

blurbs.text: The dry season lowers water levels, exposing textured mudflats and making the sawgrass prairies stand out against the sky. Clear skies make this the best time to paddle the mangrove tunnels or walk the raised boardwalks.
Early rains fill the marshes and alter the reflections in the shallow waters. Rising humidity and afternoon clouds can cut distant views across the prairies.

The wet season floods the prairies, turning the landscape into a vast, unbroken sheet of water. Heavy afternoon thunderstorms frequently block visibility and limit access to open-water kayaking and exposed trails.
The heavy summer rains taper off, leaving the wetlands fully inundated and green. Receding storm clouds open up wider views of the flooded sawgrass plains before the dry season takes hold.

gemini.depth_why: Scores change with the austral seasons, dropping in winter due to short daylight and harder access to remote areas.
gemini.overview: The Falkland Islands are known for rugged, windswept coasts and the vast, treeless expanses known as the Camp. White sand beaches contrast with dark Atlantic waters, forming the iconic coastal views of the archipelago. The best viewing conditions align with the long daylight hours from November to February.

blurbs.text: Long daylight hours illuminate the white sand beaches and rolling, treeless plains of the Camp. The coastal views are at their clearest, making it the best time to explore the rugged shorelines.
Shorter days and cooler winds cross the open landscapes. The rugged coastlines remain striking, though skies are often grayer and the light fades earlier.
Very short days and frequent frost or snow can obscure the coastal tracks and limit access to remote viewpoints across the open land.
Lengthening days bring back the stark beauty of the coastal cliffs and open plains as the ground thaws.

gemini.depth_why: Access to the cliffs and outer islands changes with the daylight and ferry schedules.
gemini.overview: The Faroe Islands are known for sheer basalt cliffs dropping into the North Atlantic and steep, treeless mountains. The signature view is Múlafossur waterfall plunging directly into the ocean below the village of Gásadalur. Visitors drive narrow coastal roads and hike to viewpoints like the summit of Slættaratindur or the sea cliffs of Mykines.

blurbs.text: Short daylight hours limit time on the trails, and winter storms frequently obscure the mountains. The coastal roads can be driven, but high winds often make cliff viewpoints difficult to reach.
Daylight lengthens rapidly, revealing the snow-dusted peaks of Slættaratindur. Trails are often muddy and some remote mountain passes remain blocked by lingering snow.
Ferries resume service to Mykines, opening access to its dramatic sea cliffs. The valleys turn green, and the waterfalls flow heavily from the spring melt.

Long summer days provide nearly endless light for driving the coastal routes and hiking to Múlafossur. The sea is calmest, allowing reliable ferry access to the outer islands and clear views from the highest summits.
Autumn brings low light that casts long shadows across the basalt cliffs. Ferries to the outer islands run reduced schedules, and low clouds settle more often over the mountain passes.

gemini.depth_why: Scores form clear groups based on the transition between the wet and dry seasons.
gemini.overview: Fiji is known for its coastal scenery of turquoise lagoons and white-sand islands. The Mamanuca and Yasawa island chains provide classic South Pacific views of palm-fringed beaches and shallow reefs visible through clear water. Inland, the larger islands like Viti Levu feature modest volcanic mountains and dense tropical forests.

blurbs.text: Heavy rains and frequent cloud cover dull the bright colors of the lagoons. Storms often churn up the water, reducing clarity for coastal views, though the inland forests grow thick and green.
The heavy rains begin to ease, and the skies clear more often. The turquoise waters regain their bright hues as the sediment settles, making the island views much sharper.

Clear skies and dry air create the best conditions for taking in the coastal scenery. The contrast between the white sand, deep blue ocean, and bright lagoons is at its sharpest, and visibility across the water is excellent.
More cloud gathers over the islands. The lagoons remain bright and striking, though occasional showers soften the distant views of the volcanic peaks.

gemini.depth_why: The islands stay the same, but a low gray mist covers them for part of the year.
